prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: EN · Plan comparison (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Feature" · longest unbreakable word 56px · one-line width 83px
  col 2: header "Free" · longest unbreakable word 79px · one-line width 79px
  col 3: header "Pro" · longest unbreakable word 66px · one-line width 66px
  col 4: header "Enterprise" · longest unbreakable word 75px · one-line width 229px
  col 5: header "Notes" · longest unbreakable word 73px · one-line width 419px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 720px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Compare three plans feature by feature, with a free-text Notes column for caveats and supporting detail.","reading":"Readers scan the Feature column down the rows, then compare Free, Pro and Enterprise across each row; Notes is read secondarily after the plan values and is not part of the main tier comparison.","groups":["Free, Pro and Enterprise are peer plan columns and should read as one comparison block.","Feature is the row-label column and should stay visually distinct from the plan values.","Notes is supplementary commentary, so its width can flex against the plan block."],"keep_intact":["Feature, Free, Pro, Enterprise headers","Community, Unlimited, Custom, 1 year, 30 days, —, ✓","SSO / SAML","24/7"],"may_wrap":["Notes prose","the long Enterprise cell 24/7 phone & dedicated manager","longer Notes such as response-time and Okta/Azure details"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[130,100,90,170,229],"idea":"Balanced publication layout: readable Feature labels, compact but intact Free/Pro columns, extra room for Enterprise, and Notes as a secondary wrapping column."},{"name":"B","widths":[125,110,110,110,264],"idea":"Peer-plan comparison: set Free, Pro and Enterprise to equal widths so the three tiers scan as a single comparable block, with Notes taking the remainder."},{"name":"C","widths":[110,100,87,100,322],"idea":"Notes-forward reference: keep plan columns near their minimum intact widths and give maximum space to Notes to reduce wrapping in the commentary column."}]}
